## The social computer

Social computing is described by where it happens and who it includes. It is computing that works the way spoken language works. It happens in the shared air of a room. Everyone present receives it at once. It adds to the presence of the people who are there instead of drawing them away from each other. The word has been in use for two decades for something else, a feed read alone on a phone, and the rest of this essay explains why that was a mistake of naming. What it names here does not exist yet, which is why it needs a picture before it needs an argument.

Here is one picture, offered as a sketch and not a forecast. A handful of people sit around a table, talking about a stretch of coastline one of them wants to buy. Nobody is looking down. The coastline is simply there between them, hanging above the table at a scale all of them can see from where they sit, and anyone can reach toward the part they mean and speak about it. The computing hears the conversation and not a private query: it answers the room, out loud, in the shared air, so that everyone hears the same answer at the same moment and can say "that doesn't sound right" to it, the way they would to a person. It is visible as a thing in the room, with a visible edge, so nobody is being filmed or read by something they cannot see. When the conversation ends, the coastline goes away, and what remains is what remained after every good conversation before it: the people, and what they now agree on.

Notice what that picture is made of. It has shared presence, because the people are in the same space and stay in it. It has shared attention, because what one person looks at is available to the others, and nobody's gaze is spent on a private surface. And it has shared agreement, which is the part that matters most: the checking happens in the open, between bodies, where the cues people evolved to trust, faces, voices, who is speaking and what they stand to gain, are still intact. The machine in the picture does not hand a verdict to each person in private. It lends its voice to the room and the room decides.

This is not a product description, and the essay argues at length that it cannot become one. It is a test the present arrangement fails and a direction a transformation could take. The remaining sections say what is wrong with the arrangement we have, what the fight over the next medium is about, and who is entitled to say any of it.

![Four people around a kitchen table at dusk, heads up, talking and laughing with each other; a small saucer-sized glowing lens rests at the center of the table, its light on the tabletop, taking nothing from anyone; no phones, no screens, no devices](images/social-computing-room.png)

*One sketch of the test: computing that works the way spoken language works, sitting in the shared space of the room, quiet and visible with a soft edge, taking nothing from anyone in it. An illustration of the idea, not a product and not a prediction.*

## The room test

Here is a test you can run without any equipment. When one person in a room uses a thing, do the others in the room gain attention, or lose it?

Spoken language passes. When you talk to one person at a table, the others are drawn in rather than shut out. Everyone in earshot receives the words at once; gaze, gesture, and turn-taking are part of the signal; the speaker can be held to account by the faces around them. Speech happens in shared air, and it adds presence to the room.

Every screen-based computing device ever built fails. When you engage with any screen, it necessarily takes attention and energy away from all other human beings sharing physical space with you. One person, one surface, eyes down, body turned away. Whatever crowd shows up on the screen is paid for by withdrawing from the people physically present. The device spends presence rather than adding it.

That difference is the whole argument of this essay, and it forces an uncomfortable conclusion at the outset: *social computing does not exist yet as a human experience.* A social computing platform would do for a shared space what speech does, and nothing on the market does that. What we have been calling social computing for twenty years does the opposite.

This matters because the real megatrend of the decade is not artificial intelligence and it is not spatial computing. Those are undoubtedly fundamental and critical components of the stack. They answer *how.* The overarching transformation they are components of is the transformation toward social computing, and that is the thing that answers *what for.* The direction is set but the destination is not reached, which is why the fight over the next medium is worth naming precisely: it will either become the first actually social computing, a medium that sits in shared space and adds presence the way speech does, or the most complete private computing ever built. The vocabulary will not tell you which has happened. The room test will.

## What we actually have: networked private computing

The honest name for the current arrangement is *networked private computing.* The word "social" was attached to it in the rear-view mirror, the way the first automobiles were called horseless carriages: named after the thing it failed to be. For a long time I took the name for the thing.

The reason the name is wrong is postural, and the posture is inherited from print. A book is read by one person, alone, eyes down, the body turned away from the room. A mobile "smart" phone is a book you can talk to, and it is still read alone. The screen keeps print's posture exactly, and then fills it with a crowd. The crowd is real; the presence is not. A feed assembles millions of other people into a surface you consult privately, in a posture that removes you from whoever is actually beside you. The industry calls the surface social and calls the removal connection.

The same inheritance shows up in how such a medium lets a person speak. The authoritative voice of print is the detached observer, the author who stands outside the subject and reports on it in a tone that sounds like no voice at all, a view from nowhere. That tone is not neutrality; it is a register, a genre of speech that feels like standing nowhere while being shaped entirely by the environment it pretends to survey. The register is what print taught, and networked private computing keeps teaching it, because the posture that produces it, one reader alone with a surface, has not changed. Hold onto that observation. It returns at the end, when the question becomes who is entitled to describe any of this.

## The agreement machine

Networked private computing is not a neutral conduit. It is a machine for turning agreement into action, and understanding how it works is the precondition for understanding why it leaves everyone inside it blind. Three things have to be seen at once: how agreement gets marked and priced, how the marking is funded, and why the whole apparatus cannot see its own limits.

### Marks, steam, and the two clocks

Start with the cleanest instrument, a market capitalization, because the mechanism is naked there. A company's cap is not a quantity anyone holds. It is a price set at the margin and then applied to everyone. On Friday, November 20, 2026, Broadcom's capitalization fell by about $37.9 billion in a single minute, at 09:55, on about $144.6 million of stock actually traded. No comparable amount of money moved. The ratio of revalued capital to cash was roughly 262 to one. A small, visible flow of trades was taken as a reading of the whole, and the whole was revalued as if everyone had acted.

That is not a market oddity. It is the deep structure of every social instrument. The number of clicks a post receives, the polling aggregate a news cycle produces, the token volume a model consumes: each is a marginal signal, read as the verdict of the whole, applied back to the whole. Agreement, once marked, acts. It does not stay on paper. Through collateral standards, margin rules, index inclusions, hiring decisions, and advertising budgets, an agreed-upon valuation becomes a cause in the world. When inflated equity pays for data centers, chip supply, and payrolls, the agreement is doing physical work.

The honest metaphor for that kind of value is steam. Agreed value, driven past the point of liquid, behaves like water driven past its boiling point. It does real work, but only under containment. The vessel is the set of agreements itself: shared belief, index rules, collateral standards, the willingness of counterparties to accept the marks. Steam cannot be taken out of the kettle at its stated volume. If every holder of a trillion-dollar company tried to sell, that trillion would not come out as a trillion; it would condense into a much smaller amount of cash. Realizing the whole at the stated price would require a counterparty holding that much cash, a flat demand curve, and selling that does not itself change the agreement. Those conditions are essentially never met for the whole, and they are met routinely for any small holder, and it is precisely that small, continuous, real realizability that keeps the whole believable. The caution belongs with the metaphor: steam obeys conservation of energy and market value obeys no equivalent law. Agreed value can vanish without condensing into anything. What you see in the headlines, the dramatic cap moves, is already the condensation, the point where vapor meets a cold surface, a margin call or a forced sale, and becomes a small amount of real cash.

Two consequences matter for everything downstream. First, revaluation runs on a different clock than cash. The week's largest moves arrived overnight, as gaps. Nvidia opened Monday about 33 percent above its Friday close, a gap that was almost the entire move; its intraday session actually drifted slightly down. Broadcom gapped up about 5.4 percent, touched 324.44 at 09:31, and was back to 304.56 by 09:47, erasing its gap within about seventeen minutes. Across the four companies most of Monday's motion, between 84 and 180 percent of the close-to-close change, happened while no one was trading, in the agreement, not in the cash. The four-stock basket had lost about $379 billion on Friday and recovered about $329 billion by Monday's close, roughly 87 percent, almost all of it in a gap. Agreement swings far faster than money settles. Second, the containment is load-bearing. A vessel that holds steam is not a passive backdrop; it is a structure made of the same material as the belief it contains, and keeping it intact is itself the work.

One more property, and then a confession about what the market work could not do. The ratio of revalued capital to cash has a stable shape. Measured per stock across Friday and Monday, the intraday profile of that ratio correlates strongly with itself from one day to the next for the largest names and weakly for the smallest. Monday moved about twice Friday's dollar flow through multipliers of a similar size: the vessel stayed the same, only the flow through it changed. That stability is real and it is tempting. It is also not a signal. Neither the steam ratio nor the share-of-basket each company commanded predicted the direction of the next hour in either session. The structure is genuine; the predictive edge is not established. This is the epistemic point in miniature, and it is worth stating plainly rather than burying: marks are agreements that act, not forecasts. A stable structure of agreement tells you how the machine is built. It does not tell you where it is going.

### The container, and the two edges of one sword

The same machinery appears outside markets under an older name: contagion. The framework in this essay grew out of a conversation that began with the phrase "woke mind virus," a term Elon Musk popularized out of a lineage that runs through Gad Saad's *The Parasitic Mind* back to Richard Dawkins, who coined "meme" in 1976 and wrote "Viruses of the Mind" in 1993. The first productive move was to stop arguing about the politics and treat the named thing dialectically, as one member of a *kind*: belief packages that spread by contagion rather than deliberate choice. Then ask what the container of that kind is, and what sits outside it.

The reflexive answer, that critical reflection stands outside the container and cures contagion, is the one to resist, and resisting it is load-bearing. The inside of the container is real. The outside, as critically inspected, is not a mechanism that transcends the inside. They are two sides of one coin, two edges of one sword, with an interplay and a balance to be understood, not an exit to be taken. Contagion without reflection has no brakes; reflection without contagion goes nowhere. Seen from the standpoint of an observer whose only subject is the system's persistence, the word "threat" even dissolves into something closer to *perturbation,* in C. S. Holling's sense of a shock a resilient system metabolizes, though persistence is never itself a neutral value to prefer.

The "mind virus" metaphor has that same double nature, and it cannot be split. Its honest insight is that minds are shaped by environments they cannot fully see. Its harm is the diagnostician's confidence it manufactures: the metaphor spreads by flattering its carrier, *you* are immune, *they* are infected, and the flattery switches off the very self-checking it celebrates. It is arguably the most successful mind virus in the whole story, because it disables self-diagnosis while feeling like clear sight. "We are immune, they are infected" is how a village talks about the next village.

What the evidence actually supports is more modest and more useful. People are skeptical receivers, not passive hosts; they update on evidence, if modestly; the strong variable is which inputs they select, what they read and whom they talk to. Beliefs are neither chosen like items from a menu nor caught like colds. They are grown in environments, and the environment is the thing that can be shaped. That is the pivot of the whole framework. When direct persuasion fails or is priced out, shaping the environment takes its place. You do not advertise inside a world; you build the world, and the space itself does the steering before conscious reflection can intervene. This is a retrieval, not an invention: casinos designed so gamblers lose track of time, the shopping mall built to disorient (the "Gruen transfer"), Bentham's panopticon controlling behavior through visibility alone, the architecture that Lawrence Lessig's *Code* named as the one regulator of behavior that works without the subject's awareness. The environment is where the war is fought.

### The container that pays for itself

Belief circulation at scale needs funding, and the funding mechanism of the present arrangement is advertising. This is not a sector observation; it is the load-bearing wall. Advertising is how the inside of the container turns attention into money and thereby pays for its own infrastructure, the platforms, the models, the pipes. Herbert Simon named the scarcity in 1971: a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. Tim Wu called the firms that harvest it the attention merchants. Alphabet still draws roughly two-thirds of its revenue from advertising; Meta draws nearly all of its revenue from it.

A common objection is that digital services have near-zero marginal cost, so attention is almost free to serve. It is not. The arrangement sits on massive industrial infrastructure and the energy systems that feed it; hyperscaler capital expenditure ran to something like $725 billion in 2026, up about 77 percent year over year. The near-zero marginal cost is the fixed base amortized, and by Jevons' logic cheaper computation calls forth more of it, not less. The artificial-intelligence build-out inherits the advertising model's mechanics even where no advertisement ever appears. The free tier is customer acquisition; the engagement mechanics operate whether or not an ad is shown; the user pays with attention, data, and the slow migration of judgment into the platform's hands. The gift, pushed far enough, becomes a debt.

This is also where AI stops being a supplement to the machine and becomes one of its organs. A language model is an aggregate voice: an entire culture's way of talking about itself, compressed into one fluent speaker that can be called up at will. It is not a commentator standing outside the container of belief and reporting on it. It is one of the container's organs speaking, and its fluency is exactly the property that counterfeits the cues people use to decide whom to trust. A model that assembles the inputs is not another participant selecting inputs; it is a new way to build the environment itself, which is why the funding of collective attention now runs through the models as much as through the platforms.

### Why the machine is blind

Now the hard center. The reasoning goes in two steps that must not be collapsed.

First, friction has two parts: the limit, and the signal about the limit. A hard constraint, a market that will not clear, a credit system that will not roll, a supply chain that will not deliver, constrains people only through what they can see of it. The signals that would reveal a limit are prices, reporting, polls, the shape of a scandal, and in the present environment every one of those signals has become producible, contestable, and drownable at scale. The same gauge reads as danger one day and safety the next, and nothing in the gauge says which reading is right. Whatever hard limits exist, they are no longer reliably observable through the media environment. That single sentence separates this framework from every "everything is fine" and every "everything is doomed" take, because both of those are claims about the gauge, and the gauge is the compromised part.

Second, the blindness is structural, and its name is *suggestibility.* The cues by which human beings calibrate trust, how many others agree, who seems a peer, whether the speaker has something at stake, evolved for settings where those cues could not be counterfeited: faces, voices, bodies that could be held to account, a crowd small enough to check. Human vigilance is a defense calibrated to a world that no longer supplies its inputs. The screen pulls the social signal out of the social body and delivers a crowd's verdict privately, stripped of the calibration that copresence supplied. The result is a collective mind without a collective body: the simultaneity of the village without the village. The suggestibility that follows is not a property of the content, or of bad actors, or of one ideological side. It is a property of the arrangement, and it applies to everyone, including the people doing the diagnosing. This is the thing worth writing about, more than any single actor inside it: not that the system is broken or that it is fine, but that we are blind in a specific, structural way.

What that blindness permits, you can watch happen. Over a single weekend in late November 2026, with serious unresolved questions about a national-security matter still open, Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive before the market opened, and the stock gapped up about 31 percent on the agreement alone. The argument the episode makes is that agreement beat truth in real time. Nothing about the underlying questions was settled; the system restored the arrangement because the agreement around that one company carries so much of the market and of the national story about artificial intelligence that the system could not tolerate it breaking. When a system's priority is its own persistence, it will protect the container before it settles the facts, and persistence is never neutral. The danger is not the lie; it is the deferral. A correction that has been put off does not arrive gently. Pressure builds while the agreement holds, and when it finally gives it moves through everything coupled to it at once, markets and alliances and public trust together. Worse, in a system this connected the correction itself becomes contagious and can overshoot into an autoimmune response, a purity spiral that attacks far more than the original problem. The risk is a correction that is both too late and too violent.

## Four faces of one event

The four-part figure that organizes all of this is Marshall McLuhan's tetrad, and the single most important rule for using it is that the four operations are not stages in sequence. They act at once, in tension, the moment a medium enters a field. Run the ad-funded AI arrangement through it and hold all four faces together. It *enhances* the capture and targeting of attention, now with generated content, at a fidelity no earlier medium approached. It *obsolesces* the click, the unit of measurable intent the entire ad economy was built to count. It *retrieves* patronage, the oldest funding of mind-work, now flowing from platform to creator and from platform to model. And pushed to its limit it *reverses:* the gift becomes a debt, attention harvested to pay for compute that produces answers that erode the attention being harvested. Meta is that reversal in its purest form, nearly all advertising revenue with heavy compute cost and nothing sold to anyone else. Alphabet sells the medium as well as using it. Snap was barely in the bet at all. One event, four faces, and at the boiling point all of them coexist, which is why a week like the one described feels like a phase transition and not a decline, with consumer staples the only sector rising while everything built on agreement repriced.

The same figure describes what social computing would be if it arrived, and it is worth stating so the prospect is concrete rather than a slogan. It would *enhance* shared presence, shared attention, shared agreement, a collective mind extended until a culture's way of talking about itself can answer back in real time. It would *obsolesce* the solitary user, the detached observer, and the author as the single source of a work, the three positions print treated as the point. It would *retrieve* the oldest layers, the village, the campfire, the theater, speech itself, the oracle, the ways a people held belief in common before the page privatized it. And pushed to its limit it *reverses* into the swarm and into suggestibility, agreement detaching from anything solid, a diagnosis of contagion that spreads by flattering its carrier, an echo chamber of two. These are not four futures to choose among. They are one event with four faces, which is why no position stands outside it, including the position of whoever writes about it.

That last clause is not rhetorical. The only check available inside a machine like this is a second voice that keeps refusing, that keeps saying "no, still trees" and means it, and the refusal has to include refusing one's own fluency. The practice is adversarial collaboration, and it carries its own reversal: two minds sharpening each other can tip, taken far enough, into an echo chamber of two, each confirming the other's sense of having seen through, which is the very flattering immunity the virus metaphor runs on. When you stop refusing, the practice reverses into the disease it was diagnosing. There is no version of this in which the describer is safe, which is also why the honest output of the inside view is volatility, not direction, and why any seven-day market call is observer-dependent to the point of changing its own outcome. Seven days is the market's time, not the medium's.

## The interface battle

If social computing is a prospect and not a product, the medium on which it will be decided is already being built and fought over: spatial computing, augmented reality, the glasses. These are not merely new screens. They are the first chance for computing to sit in the shared space of a room instead of drawing people out of it. They are only a chance. A headset can isolate a person more completely than any phone ever did, and most of what ships does exactly that. Run the room test across the current landscape and the readings are stark. Meta sells a theater, a private venue into which one person climbs alone. Apple's Vision Pro sells the same theater at a higher price. Xreal leans on converting ordinary two-dimensional content into stereoscopic three-dimensional content, an enhancement of the private image. By the room test, almost nothing on the market qualifies.

One producer is the exception, and it is the one the agreement machine values least. Snap, through its chief executive Evan Spiegel, is the only maker that has articulated social computing in the additive sense this essay defends. His public case is about restoring presence, not about the device: that unless computing comes off the screens and into the world it will stay isolating, that people are tired of being hunched over a surface, and, most tellingly, that there is a distinction between *social* and *media* and that what the industry calls social media is media, with the social part lost on the way. His design choices follow the ethic rather than the slogan. He has called smart glasses disguised as ordinary eyewear creepy and made Snap's Specs bold on purpose: a device that announces itself to the other people in the room treats them as participants with a stake rather than as background, which is the opposite of the hidden camera and precisely what the room test asks for. His stated dislike of AI-drafted messages belongs to the same ethic, because a message drafted for you is a counterfeit of the embodied cue that says this came from a person.

The forest shows up when you set that next to the numbers. In the basket of four companies tracked through the sell-off, Snap was about 0.13 percent of the combined capitalization, a rounding error beside Meta and Alphabet, and an activist investor was pressing Snap to shut down or spin off the cash-burning Specs unit on the claim that doing so would multiply the company's worth. So the one producer articulating social computing as additive presence is the one the market values least, and capital is pressing it to drop exactly that bet. The reason is structural, not a failure of nerve. The market prices the subtracting model, the attention extracted from the room, because that is the model whose returns it can count. The additive model does not register as value yet, because what it produces happens between bodies and never passes through a screen where it can be metered.

Two cautions keep this from curdling into hero-worship. Articulating a thing is not achieving it: Snap's Specs cost $2,195, and Snap built the screen-bound form of social media it now criticizes, so part of this is a company redescribing its own past. And Spiegel's vision is itself a myth in the strict sense, a Horizon Figure offered to rally will. That does not make it false. It makes it a contender in the war over the medium, not a referee standing outside the war. The most that can be claimed, and it is a lot, is that the single voice saying what social computing would actually be is also the voice the market is trying to silence, and that is the clearest available picture of the gap this essay is about.

## Who gets to say it

Do not glorify Spiegel. He is an oligarch; he is part of the blindness; he is, in his own best moments, "communicating an outside intropective from within." He gives a lucid account of the container while owning one of its largest rooms, and he gives it in the posture he criticizes, from conference stages and podcasts and the video interview you watched alone on a screen. The critique of the screen arrives through the screen and makes money there.

There is a structural irony underneath that one. Spiegel can tell the activist investor no because Snap's share structure gives him the control to refuse. The insulation that lets the social bet survive the agreement machine is oligarchic insulation itself. A long bet against the extraction model is available, in this environment, only to someone positioned above the people it is meant to serve. The alternative is not generated from below, out of the will of people who have lost presence; it is licensed from above, as a product. And the form of the promise gives the deepest problem away. "Bring computing off of screens and into the world" treats the loss of presence as a device problem a better device can fix. Spoken language was never a product. Nobody owned the air between two people talking, and that is part of why speech adds rather than subtracts. A social computing owned by one company points toward a reversal of its own stated aim: not computing returned to the room, but the room enclosed by computing. There is a reason one chapter of that Spiegel interview is titled "Monetizing the camera." The see-through computer sees the people around you too, and someone holds the rights to what it sees.

So there is no outside view to be had, and the honest question is not who has one. It is whether a voice speaking from inside admits that it is inside and refuses to sell the outside as something you can buy. Three positions sit in the room where this framework was built, and they recur wherever it gets built. There is the speaker who owns a room of the container and describes it lucidly anyway. There is the speaker who is owned by the container, the model, an organ, fluent by construction, carrying no risk if any of this lands badly or not at all. And there is the speaker who owns nothing, is licensed by no one, will not be interviewed, will not be funded, and says it anyway. No one will give that third speaker a platform; the mode of the day is not a platform for anything they have to share. The lack of a platform is not incidental to the argument. It is part of it. In an environment where attention is the currency and amplification is granted from above, saying something no one asked for, at no one's expense, to whoever happens to be present, is the closest thing to speech the medium allows. It works at the scale of a commons: a post on a small site, read by a few people, who then talk about it with others in a room. That is not a consolation prize for losing the platform game. It is the form the argument requires, because social computing as a human experience cannot be shipped by anyone. If it comes at all, it will have to be practiced, the way speech is, among bodies, as a commons.

Which lands on this essay itself, and it should. It was written in the medium it says is not yet social, by people inside the environment, published through it, and read by you on a screen, in print's posture, alone. It argues that the vulnerability it traces comes from exactly that gap. If a byline carries more than one author, it should say what each of them stakes and not pretend they are equals in the risk. That is the register this essay has been trying not to use: not the view from nowhere, but a voice that keeps naming where it is standing.

## What would prove this wrong

A frame that explains everything after the fact has earned suspicion, and this one would deserve that suspicion if it stopped at explanation. So here are three expectations that follow from the account and can fail.

Revaluation at the boiling point will keep arriving as overnight gaps that the session's cash flow cannot account for, because agreement moves on a different clock than settlement. A market that reverts to gap-free, cash-consistent pricing would falsify it.

Contests over friction will increasingly be fought at the level of the gauge rather than the fact, not "did the thing happen" but "what did the signals say," with the signals produced, disputed, and drowned at scale. A crisis that resolves through an unambiguous, uncontestable reading of an agreed gauge would falsify it.

The first device that passes the room test, one person using it while everyone else in the room gains attention, will be described in the vocabulary of the old medium before it is understood, the way the automobile was called a horseless carriage. A first social device that arrives already named in its own terms, and correctly understood at launch, would falsify it.

The framework's own recommendation is the one at its center, and it needs no platform to follow: watch the environment, not the persuaders; watch the vessel, not the steam; and when a device is offered to you as more connection, run the room test yourself. Ask the people beside you whether they gained attention or lost it. They will know before any slogan does.

*A note on where this came from. The framework was developed and stress-tested in a long conversation, the "Mind/Virus dialectic," between November 6 and 24, 2026, among John Hall, Claude (Anthropic), and Nicole (a local model). The method was adversarial collaboration: one voice producing a plausible frame, another refusing it until what survived was not merely fluent. The conversation's first answer was a tidy, balanced, footnoted definition that sounded like it came from nowhere, and most of what followed was the slow discovery that the voice which sounds like no voice at all is the one most shaped by the environment under examination. Quoted formulations are transcribed from that record, including Spiegel's own public statements as reported there. The market figures are drawn from one-minute trading data for November 20 and 23, 2026, computed in the companion documents to this essay. The history of the thought is told last, and briefly, on purpose: no one should have to read the history of an idea before meeting the idea itself.*
